chapter_theme: Kovalan ends his songs of the fisher girl whose eyes and brows kill, and Madhavi, reading a hidden meaning in them, takes the yazh in a sulk and answers: she sings the Kaveri as a wife whose grace proves her husband's straight sceptre, mocks a lover who comes to the shore on a trader's pretext, and voices a deserted shore woman who will not forget the one who forgot her and whose last trace of him the tide erases.

cast.role: son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer and courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
the river Kaveri, addressed in the songs as the Chola's wife

silappathikaram:7:122-125.reading: The third stanza tells the fisher girl that her brothers take lives with their running boats, and she takes lives with her bending brows, and warns her that, carrying her breasts with no thought for the pain she gives others or for her own state, her small soft waist will waste away and be lost.
silappathikaram:7:122-125.nuance: The refrain of the three stanzas (114-125) moves the killing from the father's net and the brothers' boats to the girl's eyes and brows: the fisher family's trade in lives becomes her inheritance. கோடும் புருவத்து makes the brow's curve itself the weapon, where the earlier stanzas used the net and the eye.

silappathikaram:7:126-129.reading: The singer says the girl who holds a coral pestle in her hand and pounds white pearls has red-lined eyes that are no blue lilies but cruel, cruel things.
silappathikaram:7:126-129.nuance: Pounding pearls with a coral pestle is a fisher household's work made precious: the girl's ordinary labour is given in the shore's own riches. The line that names her eyes is sung twice, as the song form requires.

silappathikaram:7:130-133.reading: The singer says the girl who walks as the swan walks on the flesh-smelling shore in the punnai shade has red eyes fierce to no purpose, and calls them Death, Death.
silappathikaram:7:130-133.nuance: கொன்னே, 'to no end', makes the eyes' cruelty gratuitous: they kill without aiming at anyone, which is the singer's complaint.

silappathikaram:7:134-137.reading: The singer says the girl who holds a honey-mouthed blue lily in her hand and drives the birds from the drying fish has red eyes that are not white spears and yet are fierce, fierce.
silappathikaram:7:134-137.nuance: She carries a flower as the thing she scares birds with, and the singer denies her eyes are spears only to say they are worse: the stanza's work is the reversal of a gentle gesture into a weapon, as in 126-129.

silappathikaram:7:138-141.reading: The singer tells the young swan not to follow the girl who wanders churning the wave-washed shore, since it cannot match her gait.
silappathikaram:7:138-141.nuance: This is the last of Kovalan's songs before Madhavi takes the lute. The compliment that the swan is beaten by a woman's walk is one he once paid Kannaki in their bridal chamber; here it goes to an imagined fisher girl, sung before Madhavi.

silappathikaram:7:142-153.reading: Having heard the kaanal vari, Madhavi decides that Kovalan's songs carry some hidden intent and that he has lost himself in another, and, seeming glad of their union but in a sulk, takes the yazh and, as if she too had a hidden meaning, begins to sing her own kaanal vari in a voice joined to the instrument, so that the land's deity marvels and the people rejoice.
silappathikaram:7:142-153.nuance: The whole break turns on குறிப்பு: she reads one into his songs (144) and sings as one who has her own (148). Neither intent is confirmed; the poet says only that she seemed (போல்) glad and seemed to have a meaning. The quarrel that ends the union at 286-300 begins here as two readings of songs, not as any act.
silappathikaram:7:142-153.event: Madhavi, reading a hidden meaning into Kovalan's songs, takes the yazh in a sulk and begins to sing kaanal vari of her own.

silappathikaram:7:154-161.reading: Madhavi hails the Kaveri, who walks with bees humming at her sides, wearing a garment of jewel flowers and opening her dark kayal eyes, and says she knows that all this graceful going comes from her husband's well-set sceptre not bending.
silappathikaram:7:154-161.nuance: Madhavi keeps Kovalan's figure of the Kaveri as the Chola's wife but changes what the wife's grace proves: in his stanzas (21-36) it proved her patience with his other unions; in hers it proves his justice. The epic's later turn, Kannaki's case against a king whose sceptre did bend, makes this praise of the Chola sceptre a standard the Pandya will fail.

claims.claim: a king's unbending sceptre shows in the ease and plenty of his land, as a wife's bearing shows a just husband

silappathikaram:7:162-169.reading: Madhavi hails the Kaveri, who walks as the peacock dances in the flower groves, cuckoos sing and lovely garlands sway at her sides, and says she knows all this going from seeing the strength of her husband's dread spear.
silappathikaram:7:162-169.nuance: Set beside 154-161, the second stanza grounds the same graceful flow in the king's spear rather than his sceptre: justice and force are given as two causes of one ease, stanza by stanza.

silappathikaram:7:170-177.reading: Madhavi blesses the Chola's rich land and the Kaveri who, becoming a mother who rears it like a child, never stops her great help that carries the world through the ages, and says that this unceasing flow that sustains life is the grace of the day-bringer who rules the wheel.
silappathikaram:7:170-177.nuance: ஆழி ஆள்வான் பகல்வெய்யோன் can be the sun, or the Chola as the sun who rules the wheel of command; the evening passage of kaathai 4 calls the sun the world's sole wheel-ruler, so the river's bounty is credited to a ruling power either way. ஊழி here is the age of the world, not fate.

claims.claim: the river's unfailing gift that sustains all life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel

silappathikaram:7:178-181.reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi tells the man that, though the pearls cannot match the girl's smile, he comes every day like Kama's son saying he wants the pearls the waters bring, and names their town Puhar, where the swelling tide brings shining white pearls to the fragrant shore and goes back, like traders, carrying off flower garlands.
silappathikaram:7:178-181.nuance: The man's excuse is a buyer's excuse, and the refrain makes the tide itself a merchant bartering pearls for garlands. Sung to Kovalan, a great merchant's son, the stanza mocks a lover who disguises desire as trade.

silappathikaram:7:182-185.reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi asks how simple folk like them could know that in the fishing hamlet the bangles slipping from girls' red hands proclaim those who married them in secret, and names Puhar, where swans climbing the budding punnai look like the full moon among stars and bees hum at the water lilies.
silappathikaram:7:182-185.nuance: The secret is betrayed by the girl's own wasting body: the bangles loosening on a thinning arm do the gossiping (தூற்றுவதை), so the scandal is the man's doing but written on her.

silappathikaram:7:186-189.reading: In the shore girl's voice Madhavi asks how they could know that in the hamlet where strong toddy and food never run out he would bring a girl an unending sickness without any cure, and names Puhar, where girls whose sand-houses the waves have wrecked scoop sand with their hands and, their long spear-like eyes brimming, try to fill up the sea.
silappathikaram:7:186-189.nuance: The reading turns on உறை (a cure, or a single drop?) and on how புண்தோய்வேல் and பரதர் attach in 188-189; line 189 also carries a repaired character. The image of girls weeping as they try to fill the sea that wrecked their play-houses is clear and makes a child's futile revenge the picture of the girl's grievance.

silappathikaram:7:190-193.reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells her friend of the curled five-plaited hair that the lord of the loud-waved shore, who looked at the spotted crab playing with its mate, at the flowering grove and at her, went away so that her senses left her, and she does not know his mind.
silappathikaram:7:190-193.nuance: The crab with its mate is the scene of union he watched before leaving, so the stanza sets what he saw against what he did. வண்ணம் உணரேன் is ambiguous between not knowing his nature and not knowing her own state.

silappathikaram:7:194-197.reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, asks whether he has left them, forgetting with his cool grace and his horse-drawn chariot, says let him go, and tells the soft-clustered adumbu creepers and the swans that she will not forget those who forgot her.
silappathikaram:7:194-197.nuance: The stanza turns on the shift from 'they' to 'we': he forgot, we will not forget. Sung to Kovalan, the vow of remembering is at once a lament and a reproach, which is how Kovalan hears it in 286-300.

silappathikaram:7:198-201.reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells the honey-mouthed neythal that, unlike her own eyes which weep in the sorrowful evening, it suffers no pain and gets to sleep, and asks whether in its dreams it sees the cruel man coming to the shore grove.
silappathikaram:7:198-201.nuance: The neythal closes at dusk, so the flower is said to sleep; she cannot, and so she is shut out even from the dream in which she might see him, and must ask a flower for news of it.

silappathikaram:7:202-205.reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, tells the clear tide that it has broken up every trace of the path where the wheel of his bird-swift horse-chariot went, and asks what she can do, since the tide, which stays with her and with those here, does not understand.
silappathikaram:7:202-205.nuance: The wheel-track is the last thing left of him, and the tide erases it while staying beside her: the grievance is that the sea is near her and still unfeeling.

silappathikaram:7:206-209.reading: Madhavi, in the woman's voice, asks the flower grove, the swans that play in pairs and the cool ford whether they will not tell the tide, which rolls in erasing the path of their pledged lover's tall strong chariot, that this is not right.
silappathikaram:7:206-209.nuance: நேர்ந்த, 'who pledged', makes the lover one who gave his word; the stanza appeals to the shore's creatures as witnesses to a wrong done to that pledge. The same opening line begins the next stanza (210), which carries the song on.

links.note: The couplet says her eyes would not make him tremble if her bent brows would straighten and screen them; the song says she takes lives with her bending brows, as her brothers take lives with boats.
links.teaches: In the Kural the curved brow is the eyes' failed guard, which could save him by straightening, while the song makes the curve itself the killer and the killing a family trade, so the pair shows the same conceit shifted from a hope of rescue to a charge of hereditary guilt.

gains.a: the song's brow-as-weapon gains the couplet's sense that the brow's bend is a fault, கோடு, the word for a bent sceptre too
gains.b: the couplet's private plea gains a social frame, a fisher girl whose people kill for a living, so the lover's charge of murder is cast as inherited rather than chosen

links.note: Kovalan tells Kannaki in their bridal chamber that the swan, beaten by her gentle gait, hid among the lotus pools; in the kaanal vari he tells the swan not to follow a fisher girl, whose walk it cannot match.
links.teaches: The same compliment Kovalan gave his bride is given, with Madhavi listening, to an imagined shore girl, so the pair shows how readily his praise moves from one woman to another, the very thing Madhavi then reads as a hidden meaning.

links.note: Madhavi reads a hidden intent into Kovalan's songs and sings as if she had one too; at the end Kovalan says she sang with her mind on another, and leaves her, the narrator saying his former deed had come to fruit.
links.teaches: Set together, the two passages give the break two causes: a pair of mutual misreadings of songs that the poet marks as seeming, and the ஊழ்வினை the narrator names when Kovalan goes, so choice and karma are both offered for the same parting.

links.note: The Purananuru poem tells Killivalavan that the land of the just sceptre on the Kaveri gets rain when it asks, and that kings are blamed when rains fail; Madhavi's stanza reads the Kaveri's easy flow as proof that the Chola sceptre does not bend.
links.teaches: The Sangam counsel makes plenty a duty the king must earn and warns he will be blamed for drought, while the epic song takes the river's plenty as already proving his justice, so the pair shows the counsel hardened into a courtly praise that can no longer imagine the failure the older poem warns of.

gains.a: Madhavi's figure gains its political doctrine, that a straight sceptre shows itself in the land's fertility, from an older address to a named Chola
gains.b: the poem's conditional warning gains a later reception in which the same link between sceptre and Kaveri is sung as settled fact, the form the epic later breaks with the Pandya

links.note: The couplet says it is not the spear but the unbending sceptre that gives a king victory; Madhavi's paired stanzas say the Kaveri's grace shows first her husband's unbending sceptre, then the strength of his spear.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks the sceptre above the spear and removes the spear as a cause, while Madhavi's song sets them side by side as equal signs of one prosperous river, so the pair shows the court song keeping the force the ethical couplet sets aside.

gains.a: the stanza's turn from sceptre to spear gains a measure: the Kural shows the spear stanza is the one an ethicist would refuse
gains.b: the couplet gains a contrary witness, a praise-song that will not drop the spear when it praises the just king

links.note: Pattinappaalai says the Kaveri does not fail even when the star goes south and the sky withholds rain; Madhavi's stanza says the Kaveri's unceasing help that sustains life is the grace of the ruler of the wheel.
links.teaches: The idyll makes the river's reliability its own, a guarantee standing even against a failed sky, while the epic song moves that same unfailing gift under a ruler's grace, so the pair shows the Kaveri's bounty passing from a fact of the land to a token of the king.

gains.a: the stanza's ஒழியாய் gains its older ground, the Sangam guarantee that this river does not fail when the rains do
gains.b: the idyll's praise of the river gains a later reading in which its constancy is no longer self-standing but credited to the sun-like Chola

links.note: In Kovalan's sarthu vari the shore girl asks how simple folk could know that men who broke their oaths before the sea-god are without dharma; in Madhavi's, she asks how they could know that girls' slipping bangles proclaim the men who married them in secret.
links.teaches: Both songs use the same refrain of feigned simplicity, but Kovalan's names the man's broken oath as the wrong while Madhavi's shows the cost landing on the woman's body, whose loosening bangles make the secret public, so the exchange moves blame from the oath to its visible price.

links.note: Madhavi's stanza tells of a shore lord who looked at the crab with its mate and at her and then went away, leaving her senseless; at the kaathai's end Kovalan, hearing her songs as aimed at another, lets go of her and leaves.
links.teaches: The persona's lament for a lover who left after seeing a scene of union is followed, within the evening, by the singer's own lover leaving her, so the pair shows Madhavi's song turning from a role into her situation.

links.note: The couplet's woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she knows no forgetting and even remembering burns; Madhavi's woman says to the adumbu and the swans, let him go, we will not forget those who forgot us.
links.teaches: In the Kural not forgetting is a helpless bind, since memory both burns and keeps her alive, whereas in the song it is announced as a choice with an audience, a reproach to the forgetter, so the pair shows the same refusal to forget used as a lament and as a charge.

gains.a: the stanza gains the couplet's inner cost, that the vow not to forget is also a burning she cannot escape
gains.b: the couplet's private bind gains a public turn, the same memory declared to witnesses as an accusation against the one who forgot

links.note: The couplet's woman lives because she sees in dreams the man who gives no grace awake; Madhavi's woman, whose eyes cannot sleep in the evening, asks the sleeping neythal whether it sees the cruel man coming in its dreams.
links.teaches: The Kural's comfort depends on sleep, and the song removes it: the sleepless woman is shut out of the dream that keeps the couplet's speaker alive and can only ask a flower for it, so the pair shows the dream-comfort as a privilege of those who can sleep.

gains.a: the stanza's question gains its stake: in the Kural the dream is what keeps a deserted woman alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it does not state, that its consolation fails the woman who cannot sleep at all

links.note: The Ainthinai Ezhupathu heroine asks whether the sea, like her, does not sleep because the same shore lord took his fill of it and left; Madhavi's woman tells the neythal that, unlike her, it sleeps free of pain.
links.teaches: The two neythal women look to the shore for company in sleeplessness and reach opposite answers, one finding in the restless sea a fellow sufferer, the other finding in the closed flower only a sleeper who does not share her pain, so the pair shows the same evening shore read as sympathy and as indifference.

gains.a: the stanza's envy of the flower gains a contrast with the older convention in which the shore suffers with the woman
gains.b: the Sangam poem's consoling fellow-sufferer gains a counter-case in which nature sleeps and the woman is alone

links.note: The Ainthinai Aimpathu heroine begs the crab not to walk over the tracks of her lover's chariot so she can look at them her fill; Madhavi's woman tells the tide that it has already broken up every trace of that path.
links.teaches: The Sangam heroine still holds the wheel-track and pleads with a small creature to spare it, while in the song the sea has already wiped it out and she can only ask what to do, so the pair shows the same last trace of the lover first guarded and then lost.

gains.a: the stanza gains the older poem's sense of what the track meant, all that is left to look at
gains.b: the quatrain's plea gains its sequel, the loss it feared, done not by a crab but by a tide no one can beg

source_issues: Lines 183 and 189 carry TSCII repairs (ு + ட read as ூ); 189's sense in any case turns on how புண்தோய்வேல் and பரதர் attach, so 186-189 is marked uncertain.
Lines 206 and 210 are the same line: the stanza at 206-209 and the one at 210-213 open alike and the song runs across the chapter boundary; this is the song form, not a doubled unit.
